title: Constrained decoding overhead, KV cache & batching on Private/VPC (deep dive)
transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-10-07
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Location: Zoom (Ironpeak - Redwood deep dive)
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Marco (Redwood SRE); Lena, Amit, Sofia, Ben (Ironpeak)

Auto-summary (auto notes):
- Goal: Understand overhead of enforcing strict JSON/function-calling on constrained decoding and how KV cache, batching, and quantization affect per-token latency on Ironpeak's on-prem GPU cluster (VPC/private infra).
- Agreed experiments: microbenchmarks with constrained-output modes, KV prefix reuse tests, single-request vs large-batch throughput, quantized vs full-precision latencies.
- Next: SE will run bench on customer image, share results and recommended runtime config.

Topics: constrained-output overhead, function-calling latency, KV cache hit patterns, batching SLO tradeoffs, quantization impact, VPC network considerations, on-prem GPU concurrency

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan: okay, uh welcome everyone, thanks for carving out the time. we have about 45 minutes, big thanks to Lena and team for hosting, we'll keep this practical and try to get concrete next steps.
[00:18] Lena: thanks, Jordan. quick context: we're evaluating Redwood Private for an internal assistant. main constraints: strict JSON outputs for auditability, sub-200ms P95 for short completions, and data never leaves our VPC.
[00:35] Priya: got it. can you share a little about your current infra? GPUs, batch sizes you run today, etc.
[00:44] Sofia: sure, we have a 4-node cluster - each node is 2xA100 80GB, Slurm scheduling, our service fronting is envoy inside the VPC. most of our calls are short structured responses, avg 45 tokens.
[01:02] Marco: uh small note, we also enforce KMS-backed keys, and all logs go to our SIEM; we need to ensure the runtime doesn't leak intermediate tokens in logs.
[01:12] Priya: understood. from the Redwood side we'll focus on two buckets: 1) strict-output / function-calling decoding overhead and how to minimize it, and 2) system-level levers: KV cache and batching + quantization tradeoffs in a VPC/on-prem environment.
[01:27] Amit: great. first question: when we enable strict-json mode (i.e., constrained decoding to valid JSON only), how much extra latency should we expect per token?
[01:36] Priya: good question. rough rule: constrained decoding adds two main costs: 1) computation to compute token mask and adjust logits each step, and 2) potential increase in decode length if the model needs autoregressive backtracking or longer scaffolding to produce valid structure. in our measurements on similar models, masked decoding can add ~5-20% CPU/GPU overhead per token, but wall-clock impact depends on kernel fusion.
[02:05] Priya: for smaller sequences (under 100 tokens) the overhead can be more visible — say 10-30ms per request — because you lose some batching efficiency. on large streams the relative overhead drops.
[02:17] Sofia: 10-30ms per request is... consequential for us. our P95 target is 200ms. what's the knob we can use?
[02:25] Priya: couple of levers: prefer "prefix-anchored" output where the model produces a compact payload field instead of nested verbose JSON. use the runtime's partial-validate + allowlist patterns so you only mask on the keys/structural tokens rather than full-schema token-level masking every timestep. that reduces the per-step mask computation.
[02:45] Jordan: also, function-calling often isn't the same as strict-json mode. function-calling is more like the model emits a canonical call token sequence that we parse; enforcing strict JSON (e.g., valid JSON object only) is heavier because you must ensure matching braces, commas, types. function-calls let you validate at call boundary instead of per-token strict masks.
[03:05] Amit: does that mean function-calling is faster?
[03:08] Priya: in many cases yes, because you can accept a looser prefix constraint and then do a final schema parse. but if you need guaranteed syntactic correctness mid-stream (for streaming validators), then you pay the constrained decoding overhead.
[03:22] [crosstalk] Ben: question on caching - if multiple users ask similar prompts, how much does KV cache help with strict-json workloads?
[03:31] Marco: yeah, we saw decent improvements on prefix-heavy workloads.
[03:33] Priya: KV cache helps most when prompt prefixes are identical across requests - like a shared system prompt or instruction template. for Ironpeak's case, where you have a fixed JSON schema and similar instruction, you can cache the prefix KV up to the first user-specific slot. hit rates of 40-70% are plausible for productized prompts, cutting the per-request token compute by roughly the length of the prefix.
[03:56] Priya: note: constrained decoding still runs on the decode tokens, so if you cache encoder/prefix states you don't need to recompute their logits. the mask application only starts when decoding, so overall latency reduces.
[04:10] Sofia: is KV cache compatible with quantized kernels? we plan to run 4-bit ops to save memory.
[04:18] Priya: yes, KV works with quantized execution. caveat: quantization can change token probability distributions slightly which occasionally increases required decode steps or forces longer outputs to satisfy strict schema, so you should run a quality checkset. quantization tends to give 1.2-2x throughput on decode-heavy workloads but may need temperature / output-steering adjustments.
[04:40] Lena: you mentioned batching earlier - how does batching interact with tight latency SLOs? we have performance spikes at burst times.
[04:48] Marco: we saw with other customers that batching reduces overall avg cost but increases variance; P95 gets worse if you wait to fill batches.
[04:55] Priya: exactly. the runtime supports dynamic batching policies: latency-first, cost-first, and hybrid. for P95 <200ms you'd run small batch windows (e.g., 2-6ms batching) and prefer asynchronous micro-batches. you lose some cost efficiency but keep latency. on on-prem you can also overprovision GPUs for tail capacity.
[05:16] Amit: curious about network hops in our VPC - will the Redwood Private control plane talk outside? we need to avoid egress.
[05:25] Jordan: Redwood Private can be deployed with a customer-managed control plane inside your VPC (we ship an appliance image). no outbound egress required if you opt for fully air-gapped install. in that case, latency is pure local network + GPU.
[05:38] Ben: okay good. we can't accept third-party telemetry leaving the VPC.
[05:42] Priya: for tests, we'll mirror your exact networking setup. that affects batching too — if envoy fronting introduces 2-5ms per request, that reduces available headroom for constrained decoding. factor that in.
[06:00] Lena: can you talk about fallback strategies if constrained decoding fails mid-stream? we need graceful degradation.
[06:07] Priya: typical patterns: 1) allow a permissive fallback mode that emits best-effort JSON and tag the response as "partial"; 2) use function-calling as fallback; 3) do a rapid post-process repair step where you rerun a validator and if invalid, call a small repair model or run a few constrained decode steps with a higher temperature. repair adds a couple of roundtrips but keeps UX intact.
[06:33] Jordan: in Redwood we also have automatic fallback policies: if strict-json mode exceeds a per-request latency threshold we can automatically switch that request to a more permissive decode path and mark it for downstream validation. helps maintain availability.
[06:45] Amit: nice. now concretely on microbenchmarks - what will you run during the on-prem test?
[06:52] Priya: plan: 1) baseline native decode latency (no constraints), 2) strict-json token masking per-step, 3) function-call boundary constraint, 4) quantized kernels (4-bit) for the above three, 5) KV prefix cache warm vs cold, 6) different batching window sizes (0ms, 4ms, 10ms, 25ms). we'll measure per-token latency, end-to-end P50/P95/P99, throughput, and quality regressions on your eval set.
[07:19] Sofia: that sounds perfect. how long will tests take?
[07:22] Priya: about 3-4 hours to run the whole matrix on your 4-node cluster, plus overnight runs for longer throughput sweeps. we'll bring an automated harness.
[07:33] Lena: any example numbers you can share now for similar customers? just ballpark.
[07:38] Priya: ballpark for a 2xA100 node with a medium sized model: native decode P95 ~120-160ms for short 40-token responses; strict-json may push P95 to ~160-220ms depending on mask complexity. enabling KV warm cache often drops that back by 20-40ms. quantization narrows that gap but watch for quality drift. function-calling often sits between native and strict-json in latency.
[08:07] Amit: interesting. can we do per-token telemetry so we can see where time is spent (kernel time vs mask application vs enqueue/dequeue)?
[08:15] Marco: we'd like that visibility.
[08:17] Priya: yes, Redwood Runtime exposes token-level tracing (kernel exec time, mask application time, KV lookup) and we can stream a trace for sample requests. that lives in the Console / trace export and can be sent to your SIEM if allowed.
[08:31] Ben: about logs — ensure token contents aren't sent to logs in plaintext. our policy needs redaction.
[08:36] Jordan: we support token-level scrubbing and retention policies; you can configure no-raw-token logs, only token-level metrics.
[08:42] [00:08:42] [laughter] Lena: okay, plan is to run the bench, then meet with results. can you also recommend default runtime flags for our use-case?
[08:53] Priya: recommended starting config: 
- batching window 4ms
- max batch size 32
- enable KV prefix cache for system prompt, TTL infinite for production
- use function-calls where you can instead of strict-json if business allows
- run 4-bit quant on non-critical routes, keep a full-precision fallback for critical routes
- set constrained-decoding threshold: if mask application adds >20ms, route to permissive decode with post-validate

[09:24] Lena: for the first pilot, we'll keep 2 critical routes under strict-json and rest permissive.
[09:30] Priya: perfect.
[09:33] Jordan: any competitors you're evaluating?
[09:35] Amit: yes, a couple. Anthropic and some AWS Bedrock-hosted runtimes, and internal self-serve using open-source runtime.
[09:43] Priya: ok noted. Redwood's differentiation here is the combined runtime + control plane inside your VPC and the token-level tracing for constrained paths.
[09:53] Ben: security checklist we'll need: SOC2 letter, KMS integration doc, air-gap install steps.
[09:59] Jordan: we'll share those after the call.
[10:03] [silence / typing]
[10:06] Lena: last thing - cost: constrained decoding + small batching will increase unit cost, will that be visible in Console?
[10:14] Priya: yes. Console shows token-level cost breakdown, mask/mask-compute cost, and GPU utilization per route so you can attribute cost to strict routes.
[10:24] Jordan: okay, let's summarize and action items.
[10:28] Priya: quick recap: we agreed to run the benchmark on your infra with the matrix I mentioned, we'll gather traces and quality metrics, and then propose runtime tuning. we'll also deliver security docs and a pricing sketch.
[10:42] Lena: timeline?
[10:44] Priya: preliminary bench results 1 week; full report 2 weeks.
[10:49] Jordan: perfect. thanks everyone.
[10:52] [call ends]

-- End of transcript --
